PFAS Treatment’s Next Constraint Is the Residual Contract

PFAS treatment is usually described as an equipment problem. Utilities test groundwater, choose granular activated carbon, ion-exchange resin, reverse osmosis or nanofiltration, and install enough vessels to bring finished water below a regulatory limit.

By Bottleneck Briefs · Published 2026-07-02 · 13 min read

In brief

  • 2029 remains the baseline PFOA/PFOS compliance date; 2031 is conditional and proposed.
  • Yorba Linda operates 22 ion-exchange vessels with capacity of up to 25 MGD.
  • 12,300 tons/year is Calgon Carbon’s announced reactivation addition for Q1 2028.
  • Bellmawr shows spent resin can already be routed to permitted hazardous-waste incineration.

The plant is only the visible half

The molecule does not disappear when the treated water leaves the plant. Adsorption and membrane systems move PFAS into spent carbon, exhausted resin, regeneration brine or membrane concentrate. The operator then needs a facility willing and legally able to accept that residual, a contractor to move it, and evidence showing what happened after acceptance.

That second transaction is less visible than the plant itself. It is also less standardized.

EPA’s April 2026 interim, nonbinding guidance lists reactivation, thermal treatment, landfilling and underground injection among the available management routes. The document does not create a single required endpoint. It instead leaves utilities and contractors to navigate facility permits, state rules, waste profiles, transport distances, analytical requirements and future liability. (EPA interim destruction-and-disposal guidance)

The defensible commercial claim is therefore narrower than a nationwide disposal shortage. Residual handling is a plausible selective sequential constraint: it becomes important after utilities have solved the more visible problems of financing, site footprint, water chemistry, media qualification and construction. It has not yet been shown to be a fleet-wide bottleneck or an established source of pricing power.

The buildout is becoming a fleet problem

Orange County illustrates the scale transition. A 2021 ASCE account cited 35 planned treatment systems and roughly $275 million of capital spending after PFAS contamination affected nearly 60 wells. Those numbers were estimates at that time, not final completed-program expenditure, but they show how quickly a contaminant-removal project can become a regional portfolio of operating assets.

Yorba Linda moved from construction beginning in March 2021 to operation in December 2021. Its plant uses 22 ion-exchange vessels arranged in 11 lead-lag trains and can treat up to 25 MGD. That delivery record matters because it cuts against the strongest version of the residual thesis: residual acceptance did not visibly prevent the project from starting. (Yorba Linda Water District)

Other Orange County systems followed different layouts. Fullerton’s Kimberly Well 1A project used four ion-exchange vessels and was estimated at approximately $3.65 million in 2020. Tustin’s Main Street plant later combined four off-site wells through approximately 2.5 miles of conveyance pipeline and disclosed capacity of up to 6,400 gallons per minute, equivalent to 9.216 MGD. Santa Clarita Valley Water completed the Santa Clara–Honby facility in summer 2024 at a reported cost of $11.5 million, restoring approximately 2,000 gallons per minute of average production.

The common feature is not one technology. It is the creation of a growing installed base that will eventually require repeated sampling, media replacement, hauling and residual routing.

Media life changes the cadence, not the obligation

A longer-lasting adsorbent can materially reduce operating burden. It lowers the number of changeouts, truck movements and replacement-media purchases over the life of a plant.

Orange County’s pilot work demonstrates how large that variation can be. At the tested site, Evoqua PSR2+ reached initial PFOA breakthrough after 7.1 months, while Calgon CalRes 2301 and Purolite PFA694E each reached it after 4.3 months. Cyclopure DEXSORB+ reached the same site-specific threshold after 2.7 months. These were pilot results under particular influent and empty-bed contact-time conditions, not universal media lifetimes. (OCWD PFAS pilot report)

The commercial consequence is still clear. Media selection controls how often the utility encounters the downstream market.

That makes flexible vessel architecture valuable. De Nora’s system for Hampton Roads Sanitation District’s Nansemond SWIFT project is designed to accommodate different media and extend bed exhaustion before changeout. The utility can preserve its equipment investment while changing the consumable layer as performance data, regulation or residual economics evolve.

Equipment suppliers can retain relevance through that flexibility even when value migrates among carbon, resin and future media vendors. The installed vessel does not necessarily lock the utility into one residual pathway.

Regeneration changes the residual, not the obligation

Single-use resin simplifies operations at the wellhead. The contractor removes exhausted media, installs replacement resin and sends the old material to an approved outlet.

Bellmawr is the cleanest public example in the report. Veolia’s case materials describe a temporary PFAS-selective anion-exchange system with an expected 12–15 month replacement interval and spent resin routed to incineration. A later company account said the permanent system, installed in March 2023, had not yet required a media exchange as of February 2026 and would use permitted hazardous-waste incineration when replacement became necessary. (Veolia Bellmawr case)

That arrangement is operationally elegant because the utility can contract away the endpoint. It is also a strong counterexample to the idea that residual handling is already blocking deployment. What remains undisclosed is the incinerator identity, tonnage, price, queue time, manifest and liability allocation.

Regenerable resin reduces the mass of discarded media but creates another concentrated stream. SERDP’s Willow Grove work found that regeneration required salt brine and a high methanol concentration. Lifecycle performance depended heavily on solvent recovery, residual mass and the treatment of brine or still bottoms. Under the tested baseline assumptions, single-use PFAS-selective resin performed better than the regenerable alternatives. (SERDP Willow Grove project)

An Australian case offers a more favorable result. An ECT2-authored, vendor-affiliated paper reported five remediation systems, one municipal system and 26 regeneration cycles since 2019 without observed PFAS accumulation or resin-bead degradation. The case shows that repeated regeneration is technically possible. It does not provide independent U.S. municipal cost data or a complete public record of concentrate disposal.

Regeneration therefore moves the control point. It does not eliminate it. The relevant supplier becomes the operator that can regenerate media, recover chemicals, treat the concentrated stream and document the full mass balance.

Qualified capacity is the scarce product

Counting facilities is not enough. A combustor, landfill or Class I well only matters if it is permitted for the relevant stream, willing to accept it, technically qualified, geographically reachable and available when the utility needs a changeout.

EPA reported 886 Class I wells in the United States in its 2026 guidance: 745 non-hazardous municipal or industrial wells and 141 hazardous wells. It also said there is no national inventory showing which wells can or will accept PFAS-bearing material or off-site waste. Geographic distribution and facility-specific permits limit the usefulness of the headline count.

Thermal treatment has a similar distinction. Clean Harbors reported strong destruction performance from a November 2024 commercial-scale test at its Aragonite facility. EPA described results from qualifying hazardous-waste combustors as promising but stopped short of defining universal adequate operating conditions. Products of incomplete combustion, mineralization and waste-form-specific performance still require facility-level evidence.

The emerging bottleneck, where it appears, is therefore qualified capacity, not merely physical capacity.

EPA’s illustrative cost table shows why route selection can change operating economics. For a 21,000-pound media example with specified assumptions, disposal plus replacement was estimated at $1.63 per pound for off-site GAC reactivation, $2.21 for landfill and $3.35 for incineration. These are EPA illustrative 2024-dollar examples, not current market quotations.

Calgon Carbon’s response is to build capacity. Kuraray announced approximately $100 million of investment to add 12,300 tons per year of reactivated-carbon capacity in Columbus, Ohio, targeting first-quarter 2028 operations. (Kuraray-Calgon expansion)

If that project starts on schedule and available capacity remains ahead of demand, GAC residual handling may never become broadly tight. If the capacity is heavily committed, geographically insufficient or accompanied by long turnaround times, the investment will instead confirm that closed-loop service is becoming strategically important.

The value pool sits in service and risk transfer

A PFAS plant distributes spending across several layers. Engineering firms design and permit it. Equipment suppliers sell vessels, pumps and controls. Carbon and resin companies provide consumables. Contractors perform sampling and changeouts. Transporters move the residual. Reactivation kilns, combustors, landfills or injection operators provide the endpoint. Laboratories produce the documentation.

The recurring opportunity grows as the installed base ages. Initial construction spending gives way to media replacement, field service, transport, testing and endpoint fees.

The strongest commercial position may belong to an integrated contractor that guarantees treatment availability rather than simply selling media. Such a contract could cover breakthrough monitoring, replacement inventory, maximum outage, spent-media title, transport, a primary and backup endpoint, manifests, analytical verification and changes in regulation.

That conclusion remains an inference. Public records do not yet show PFAS-specific service margins, endpoint premiums, capacity-reservation fees, insurance costs or recurring contract profitability.

This distinction matters when mapping listed-company exposure. Ecolab owns Purolite, which supplies PFAS-selective resin. Xylem owns Evoqua and has a broader water-service platform. Kuraray owns Calgon Carbon and is funding new reactivation infrastructure. Clean Harbors owns hazardous-waste assets and markets PFAS treatment and disposal services. Veolia integrates water treatment and residual service. Tetra Tech and other engineering firms participate in design and construction management. LANXESS sells ion-exchange products across PFAS, micropollutants, fluoride wastewater and ultrapure-water applications.

These are positions in the chain, not proof of PFAS-specific earnings power. Companywide service revenue and hazardous-waste segment margins cannot be treated as PFAS margins. Freight, disposal and laboratory charges may also pass through an integrator’s invoice without producing much net economic value.

Control migrates only when a supplier accepts meaningful performance or liability risk.

The market may clear before the bottleneck bites

The strongest counterargument is straightforward: commercially available outlets already exist, successful plants are operating, and industry is adding capacity before the largest expected changeout wave.

Yorba Linda reached operation in nine months from the beginning of construction. Bellmawr externalized spent-resin handling through a vendor service model. Santa Clara–Honby restored wells in 2024. Tustin dedicated its centralized plant in 2025. Durham entered progressive design-build procurement in 2026. None of these public records identifies residual acceptance as the cause of a major delay.

Other constraints can remain more important. Dense urban sites may favor ion exchange because GAC requires more vessel volume. Complex water chemistry can force pretreatment or make carbon and membranes more attractive than resin. Financing, grants, permitting and civil construction determine whether the plant exists at all.

The market may also adapt through bundling rather than value migration. Established water companies can add media replacement and residual management while retaining the customer relationship. Carbon incumbents can defend share through reactivation. Equipment suppliers can preserve their installed base through media-flexible designs. Hazardous-waste firms can move upstream into profiling, logistics and documentation.

Under that outcome, residual handling becomes a recurring commercial category but remains competitive and largely pass-through. Utilities pay for it without surrendering strategic control.

The thesis would be wrong in its stronger form if several unrelated utilities publish routine first and second changeouts completed through their original outlets, at predictable prices and without material delays, substitutions or indemnity disputes.

The closest base rate favors centralized relief

The closest historical analogue is centralized GAC reactivation for conventional water-treatment media. Large users developed off-site thermal reactivation networks, bulk transport and long-term service arrangements rather than building a kiln at every treatment site.

That pattern suggests a likely resolution for part of the PFAS market: regional specialists aggregate media, operate capital-intensive infrastructure and return qualified carbon to customers. Calgon’s Columbus expansion follows that model.

PFAS differs in two important ways. Destruction and mineralization claims attract more analytical scrutiny, and long-tail liability is more salient because PFOA and PFOS are CERCLA hazardous substances. Existing infrastructure can absorb the physical process while contracts and evidence remain less standardized.

Conventional ion exchange offers a second base rate. Regeneration historically converted a large media-replacement problem into a smaller, concentrated brine problem. PFAS follows the same mass-balance logic, but its persistence and liability make the concentrated stream harder to dismiss as an ordinary waste cost.

The base rate therefore argues against permanent physical scarcity. It supports the narrower view that specialized infrastructure and service markets will expand, while qualification, documentation and risk allocation determine how quickly the market clears.

The analogy to UPW and AMR is narrow

Semiconductor ultrapure-water systems already use ion exchange, reverse osmosis, reclaim and brine recovery to move impurities into controlled residual streams. Samsung Austin has reported chemical, solids and water-use reductions from ion-exchange conversion and brine-recovery projects. LANXESS markets resins across PFAS, micropollutants, fluoride wastewater and ultrapure-water applications.

That establishes vendor and process adjacency. It does not establish that PFAS-like residual acceptance is a binding constraint inside semiconductor fabs.

The antimicrobial-resistance analogy is earlier still. WHO and UNEP treat wastewater and manufacturing waste as part of the environmental AMR problem, but the dominant treatment architecture and residual obligations remain unsettled.

Both analogies become commercially relevant only when projects create explicit requirements for concentrated-residual handling, endpoint qualification and proof that treatment did not merely transfer the hazard.

What to watch

  • 2027-12-31: EPA issues final action on the proposed PFOA/PFOS compliance-extension rule.
  • 2028-06-30: Calgon confirms commercial startup or a revised date for the Columbus expansion.
  • 2028-12-31: A public utility contract allocates spent-media title and identifies a primary endpoint.
  • 2029-06-30: HRSD reports commissioning or schedule revision for the Nansemond SWIFT facility.
  • 2031-12-31: Three unrelated utilities publish routine changeouts without endpoint substitution or unbudgeted escalation.
